title: Having a Decision Rule for a 100-Mile-Per-Hour Fastball
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Using the physics of hitting a 100-mile-per-hour fastball, which reaches home plate in about 0.4 seconds, this piece argues that elite performance under extreme time pressure depends on pre-decided decision rules rather than in-the-moment analysis. Because a batter cannot consciously deliberate in the available time, hitters convert the decision into an if-then reflex, set long before the pitch: swing at anything likely to land in the preferred zone. The author extends this to leadership, citing research on firefighters, pilots, and ICU nurses showing that under real-time pressure no one weighs options analytically; instead, top performers match the situation to a pre-loaded pattern. The practical takeaway is that leaders should identify their own recurring high-pressure situations (a hostile board question, a customer threatening to leave, a 2 a.m. system outage) and write decision rules for them in advance, including what values can't be compromised, before the pressure moment arrives.
points: The core physical fact anchoring the argument: a 100 mph fastball reaches home plate in roughly 0.4 seconds, leaving the batter less time than that to recognize the pitch and decide whether to swing, which is faster than conscious deliberation can handle.

Research on firefighters, pilots, and ICU nurses is cited to generalize the finding beyond sports: under real-time pressure, no one weighs options analytically, and top performers instead match the situation to a pattern and fire off a pre-loaded response.

The piece reframes decision rules as constraining 'the brain to what it can do in the time available,' converting an impossibly fast, high-stakes judgment into a simple if-then reflex rather than a fresh analysis.

The practical leadership takeaway is concrete: pre-decide what the 'sweet spot' looks like, what risks are acceptable, and what values can't be compromised for recurring high-pressure situations, then write, test, and revise those rules before the pressure moment arrives.
quotes: The ball reaches home plate in roughly 0.4 seconds from release. The batter has much less time than that to recognize the pitch and decide whether to swing.
So they rely upon a clear decision rule made long before the pitch is thrown: Swing at any ball likely to land in their preferred swing zone.

Studies of firefighters, pilots, and ICU nurses suggest that under real-time pressure, no one weighs options analytically. What separates the best of them is matching the situation to a pattern and firing off a pre-loaded response.
Decision rules constrain the brain to what it can do in the time available. The hitter isn't winging it when the pitch is thrown. They simply apply the decision rule.
Those who excel have pre-decided what the sweet spot looks like, what risks they are willing to take, what values can't be compromised, and what choices offer the highest probability for success.

The best leaders and the best hitters aren't distinguished by skills and talent alone. They stand out for having decided, ahead of time, exactly what they will do when the moment gives them no time to decide.
